Friday was my last day at Anthropic.

Two years ago, when Claude Code was a small internal tool, I asked it to build an RL env. I steered it for tens of hours but never manually wrote a line of code. It worked, I was hooked, and I joined the team.

Today, the default is trusting Claude's judgment to auto-approve. Claude does large migrations and builds new products. 

Helping build Claude Code into an industry-defining product has been the journey of a lifetime. 

Thank you to the incredible team behind Claude Code, Cowork, and Tag. These products are the sum of thousands of great ideas from you. I'll miss working with you all.

Thank you to our users for embracing a new way of working. Your constant feedback shaped so much of what we shipped and your stories made the work so meaningful.

Excited to see what you all make next!

tweets.text:
The divergence in AI output weirdly may be the highest it’s ever been, even though adoption is the broadest it’s ever been. 

A few years ago the best productivity gains you could get, even in the most capability-aligned field (like coding), was maybe 30-50% better productivity if you were very good at it. You’d spend a decent chunk of time cleaning up the mistakes of models, the context windows were too limited to do any long running work, and the interfaces required highly synchronous interactions. 

Now, the models can do far longer tasks at a time with limited human interaction. The harnesses support agentic work that can take on these larger tasks. The models are trained on vastly better datasets for a growing array of domains so you have to intervene far less. And we have systems that better support working with many agents at once. 

In just a two year timespan, the upper limits on productivity gains have gone from 30-50% to now likely 5-10X depending on the field. So we’ve gone from an environment where living at the frontier vs. not paying attention at all could be an order of magnitude difference in your output.

This distance is only getting wider from here given the rate of progress we’re likely to see with RSI. Crazy times.

而现在，AI模型可以更长时间地完成任务，人与机器的互动少了很多。而且，AI的训练数据质量大幅提升，涉及的领域也越来越多，你需要干预的情况更少。只用了两年，生产力的提升幅度从30-50%飙升到了现在的5到10倍，视具体领域而定。换句话说，关注AI的人和不关注的人在工作效率上差距越来越大，未来只会越来越明显。真是疯狂的时代！

tweets.text:
The divergence in AI output weirdly may be the highest it’s ever been, even though adoption is the broadest it’s ever been. 

A few years ago the best productivity gains you could get, even in the most capability-aligned field (like coding), was maybe 30-50% better productivity if you were very good at it. You’d spend a decent chunk of time cleaning up the mistakes of models, the context windows were too limited to do any long running work, and the interfaces required highly synchronous interactions. 

Now, the models can do far longer tasks at a time with limited human interaction. The harnesses support agentic work that can take on these larger tasks. The models are trained on vastly better datasets for a growing array of domains so you have to intervene far less. And we have systems that better support working with many agents at once. 

In just a two year timespan, the upper limits on productivity gains have gone from 30-50% to now likely 5-10X depending on the field. So we’ve gone from an environment where living at the frontier vs. not paying attention at all could be an order of magnitude difference in your output.

This distance is only getting wider from here given the rate of progress we’re likely to see with RSI. Crazy times.

tweets.text:
Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

tweets.text:
Increasingly this will be the new job description for a lot of roles, not just coding. We’re clearly moving from a world where agents help us do our work incrementally better or faster, to us helping agents do their work.

This turns everyone in one of these positions to that of a manager of a team of agents, instead of an individual contributor with just some added leverage from AI. The biggest areas of impact will be information-heavy jobs, like coding, cybersecurity, legal work, biotech, engineering, and many other fields. 

And as a result, in these jobs your leverage will begin to be decoupled from the normal ratio of hours spent working to output generated. For essentially the history of knowledge work the main variable you had to play with was hours of work done (assuming fixed level talent/coordination/strategy). 

Now we’ve separated these variables because agents can parallelize work for us, to in theory execute as much as we need to pull off whatever goal we’re trying to accomplish. The people and organizations that discover this sooner, and orient their operations around it, will see compounding gains in their workflows.

tweets.text:
This is one of the better litmus tests for whether you’re pushing your use of AI enough or not. 

Up until maybe six months ago probably the best you could do with AI was pull off something you already would produce, but just doing it a little faster. But now we’re entering a point where the output of working with AI can and should dramatically exceed what you would been able to do before, in a fraction of the time.

The product prototype should not only be fully functional and interactive, but it should probably have meaningfully better features than it would have had before. The engineering architecture should be able to deliver performance gains that you wouldn’t have been able to go after otherwise. 

The research for a project should consume every single fact on the subject across every dimension of analysis possible. The business process you implement with AI should operate entirely differently and learn from all its past failures in a way no human could. 

We’re unquestionably entering a period where AI will be smarter than us on most axes. Perhaps not on every dimension that matters (intelligence is still very jagged), but at least on enough dimensions that when we combine it with what we’re good at, you get qualitatively different outcomes.

So the simple test is: if you could have done what you’re doing before AI, you’re likely not pushing it enough.
tweets.summary_zh: 如果你用 AI 做的事情跟以前人能做到的差不多，那说明你没有充分利用 AI 的潜力。现在的 AI 不仅能让你工作得更快，还能做到以前无法实现的功能和效果。所以，如果你所做的事情和以前一样，那就要 rethink （重新思考）一下了！

tweets.text:
It’s almost incomprehensible how wide the distance is between someone who’s working at the frontier with AI and basically everyone else right now. 

The crazy thing is these lines are not converging, but only growing farther apart. If the curve of AI progress had leveled off, it would certainly have given most people and companies time to catch up or implement their workflows in a standardized way. The technology would have neutralized competitive advantage because everyone would be using it the same way.

But what’s happened is the opposite. The curve of AI progress is basically going vertical right now, which means if you had codified your processes 3-6 months ago you’re likely already behind again. Now imagine most companies that kicked into gear a year ago and thought that they were done. Even further behind now.

I’ve never seen a technology in my life and career that improves at this rate, which consequently means you need to upgrade your expectations at a similar rate. Our brains weren’t wired for this, and our organizational change management processes certainly weren’t either.

With any form of recursive self improvement, things just get wilder. It’s a time when you will need to be constantly reevaluating the things that didn’t work just a couple months ago to see if they now can be solved. AI native companies certainly have a strong advantage due to this right now, so now it comes down to can the bigger companies keep up. Wild times.
tweets.summary_zh: 现在，正在研究人工智能（AI）前沿的人和绝大多数人之间的差距非常大，而且这个差距还在不断扩大。之前如果技术进步放缓，大家就能慢慢跟上，但现在AI的发展速度非常迅猛，几个月前制定的流程可能现在就已经过时了。很多公司以为自己已经跟上了，可实际上他们比之前还要落后。我们需要更新对技术发展的期待，但很多人和组织都还没有准备好。现在是一个需要不断重新评估和调整的时代，AI领域的公司有很大优势，接下来大公司能否跟上就成了关键。真是个疯狂的时代！

I think world models are still in the GPT 3.5 era, but not for long.

Like the old Will Smith eating spaghetti videos, world models are impressive but not quite there yet. You can see it in the reel below, which has a mix of my Genie 4 generations and Google's.

But once they hit the GPT-5 or GPT-6 stage, I think they'll have massive implications for a lot of industries:

Movies - A big effects shot like a dragon battle takes a VFX studio months of work. With a great world model, a director could create a single frame and have AI generate the full scene from it.

Games - From my time working in gaming, I learned the real work is core loops, progression systems, and the mechanics that make a game fun. World models are already good at graphics and sound, but the gameplay isn't there yet. Still, they'll make it much easier for anyone to build their own game that looks and sounds amazing.

Just like the rise of personal apps, I think world models (along with good coding models) could make creating your own game as fun as playing a mass market one which again has huge implications.

📌 Watch my full Genie 4 tutorial to see how I created the worlds in the reel below: https://t.co/GvzPewT5gj

tweets.text: https://t.co/9JFKOz3lEv

augmenting human intellect

when i started making software, i wasn’t dreaming of a factory.

i loved that something on a screen could become an extension of my mind. a place to put a thought before i understood it. to move things around until new connections appeared. to make little systems that worked the way i worked, even if it made no sense to anyone else.

the computer wasn’t interesting because it could do work without me. it was interesting because of what i could do with it.

the early lineage of computing was built around this possibility. in 1962, Engelbart described augmenting human intellect as helping a person understand complex situations and find solutions that were previously out of reach. his starting point was the human being, not the autonomous machine.

he wasn’t describing a faster black box. he was looking at the whole relationship between a person, their tools, their language, their methods, and what they could learn to do with them. the capability belonged to that whole system.

somewhere along the way, we started telling a much smaller story about a much more powerful technology.

more automation. more agents. more software producing more software. more output from fewer people. more growth. more numbers to prove that something is happening.

and less attention to the person any of this is supposed to be for.

i don’t want to pretend computing had a pure innocent beginning. replacing human labor was one of its ambitions. even in 1960, Licklider distinguished human-computer symbiosis from systems where the remaining people mainly served the machine. he wanted computers to participate in the formation of ideas, not only execute problems already defined.

that distinction feels important – does the system help you discover what you mean? or does it only want you to submit a request, and wait outside while it works?

sometimes waiting is exactly what i want. please do the search. move the files. take away the repetitive work.

but not everything difficult is overhead.

sometimes moving the pieces around is how you understand them. sometimes making the thing changes what you wanted to make. sometimes you need to see the wrong version, touch it, take it apart, and discover a better question.

i want tools that leave room for that relationship.

in his 1981 paper on Smalltalk, Ingalls described a system meant to support everyone’s creative spirit. personal mastery mattered: an individual should be able to comprehend the system, rather than remain dependent on something permanently beyond their reach.

he also argued that computer models should fit the human mind, rather than demand the reverse.

not one perfect workflow for everyone. systems that different people can inhabit differently. someone who thinks through pictures. someone who needs to write. someone who understands a problem by building a simulation. someone whose way of organizing their life doesn’t resemble a SaaS dashboard.

a system you can reshape as your understanding changes.

this is what i want AI to make possible. not just pumping out software, but having a living relationship with it. being able to ask why something works this way. change one part without surrendering the rest. see what happened. undo it. learn enough to make the next change yourself.

the machine can become more capable without making the person smaller.

but that won’t happen just because we make the models better. we have to care about it. design for it. notice when we are making someone more dependent while calling it empowerment.

i don’t want to measure the future only by how much work happens without us.

i want to know what becomes possible for the person who couldn’t participate before.

what can they understand now? what can they express? what can they change without asking permission?

when i say augmenting human intellect, that is what i mean.

not a world that no longer needs us.
a world we have more ability to shape.
